one_liner: ByteDance's JIT- and SIMD-accelerated Go JSON library; about 1.9-3.4x the throughput of encoding/json on amd64.
what_it_does: Sonic is a Go JSON library that replaces encoding/json's Marshal/Unmarshal with a JIT/SIMD implementation. It keeps the same function signatures and adds preset configs (ConfigDefault, ConfigStd, ConfigFastest) plus a streaming Encoder/Decoder. It also has an ast.Node API that searches and modifies JSON by path without a full decode (gjson/sjson style), and an ast.Visitor SAX-style API that decodes straight into your own types. Changing the import usually works, but ConfigDefault does not escape HTML or sort map keys, so use ConfigStd when you need encoding/json output.
how_it_is_fast: On first use of each Go type, Sonic JIT-compiles a codec for that type from its reflected schema, using golang-asm on amd64. The codec is cached in an open-addressing hash with RCU and uses a register-based internal call convention. This avoids the reflection and interface/function-call overhead that limits encoding/json and jsoniter-style codecs. The hot kernels (string scan/quote/unquote, f64toa/i64toa, number parsing, skipping, UTF-8 validation) are written in C, compiled with Clang, and translated to Plan 9 assembly by asm2asm. At runtime, cpuid picks the AVX2 or SSE build (NEON on arm64), and SIMD is combined with scalar code for short inputs. The ast package parses lazily and uses SIMD skipping, so a partial Get or Set parses only the path it needs.
when_to_use: Long-running amd64 Linux/macOS/Windows services where JSON takes a large share of CPU. The JIT compile cost is paid once per type and then amortized.
Generic interface{}/map[string]any payloads. On the README's 13 KB document with std-equivalent options, generic decode is 1.9x and generic encode 3.3x encoding/json.
Struct binding on medium-to-large documents on amd64. Binding decode is 3.4x std on the 13 KB document, and 594 vs 102 MB/s on the 635 KB Twitter file (README chart).
Reading or patching a few fields of a large document without a full decode (ast.Get/Set, GetByPath). The README shows GetOne at 3,276 ns/op vs gjson at 9,431, and SetOne at 9,571 vs sjson at 36,456.
High-concurrency encoders. In the README, parallel struct encode with std options reaches 8,810 MB/s vs 3,486 MB/s for encoding/json.
when_not_to_use: arm64 servers (Graviton, Ampere, Apple silicon). arm64 has no JIT: decoding uses the interpreted 'optdec' decoder and encoding uses a VM. Maintainers say schema-typed encode is weaker there, and users report cases slower than encoding/json (issues #785, #786).

Code that must match encoding/json byte for byte or in error-state behaviour. The Go 1.27 compatibility doc lists open ConfigStd gaps. Examples: map values are merged instead of replaced, and the JIT decoder writes fields before a later syntax error. The ',string' number grammar differs, and MarshalJSON errors are not wrapped in *json.MarshalerError.

Short-lived CLIs, serverless cold starts, or latency-sensitive first requests over many or very deep types. JIT compilation happens on first use: issue #138 measured a 3.5 s first Marshal/Unmarshal on a very deep struct. The README warns that huge schemas can cause request timeouts or OOM unless you call PretouchMany first.

Teams that adopt a new Go release on day one, or that run old or exotic CPUs. Sonic depends on private runtime layouts (moduledata, map iterator), and Go 1.24.0 is unsupported. On go1.28+, non-amd64/arm64 targets, or arm64 with Go below 1.20, Sonic silently becomes encoding/json. Issue #983 (open) reports SIGILL in the SSE path on a Core 2 Quad CPU without PCLMULQDQ.

Memory-tight struct decoding. In the README, binding decode allocates 28,302 B/op vs 10,576 B/op for encoding/json. Pooled encode buffers can stay large under high QPS when large and small documents are mixed (issue #614).

integration.dependencies: github.com/bytedance/sonic/loader, github.com/bytedance/gopkg, github.com/cloudwego/base64x, github.com/klauspost/cpuid/v2, github.com/twitchyliquid64/golang-asm, golang.org/x/arch (no cgo; the native kernels ship as pre-generated Go assembly)
integration.min_toolchain: Go 1.18 (go.mod); the README lists Go 1.18-1.27 as supported; Go 1.24.0 is excluded unless you build with -ldflags=-checklinkname=0; arm64 needs Go 1.20+; Go 1.28+ currently falls back to encoding/json
integration.platforms: amd64 (JIT, AVX2 or SSE kernels chosen by cpuid; SONIC_MODE=noavx forces SSE) and arm64 (NEON kernels, no JIT, Go 1.20+), on Linux, macOS and Windows; all other targets fall back to encoding/json
integration.thread_safety: Top-level Marshal/Unmarshal and frozen Config APIs are used concurrently (the README has parallel benchmarks, and the codec cache is described as concurrent-safe with open addressing and RCU). ast.Node is not safe for concurrent reads because it loads lazily; call LoadAll() or use the ConcurrentRead search option first. Crashes during concurrent first-time JIT decodes (#912 on Go 1.24+, #985 on Go 1.27.1 amd64) were closed in Aug-Sep 2026.
integration.drop_in_for_baseline: partial — same Marshal/Unmarshal/Valid signatures and a ConfigStd preset, but ConfigDefault skips HTML escaping and map-key sorting, and decoded strings alias the input buffer. The public Decoder lacks Token/InputOffset, and ConfigStd still has documented edge-case differences (see when_not_to_use).

gotchas: Decoded strings without escapes point into the source buffer (CopyString is off in ConfigDefault). Caching the decoded objects keeps the whole JSON buffer alive; the README estimates 20-80% extra memory. Enable CopyString or ConfigStd for long-lived data.

Fallback is silent. On an unsupported arch, an unsupported Go version (go1.28+ today), or arm64 with Go below 1.20, you get encoding/json with Sonic's API, and Pretouch does nothing. Check sonic.APIKind == sonic.UseSonicJSON in CI or at startup.

Validation shortcuts: when skipping unknown fields, the SIMD path does not check escape sequences in long strings, so ConfigStd accepts invalid escapes such as '\0' (#938, open). NoValidateJSONSkip and NoValidateJSONMarshaler (in ConfigFastest) turn off more checks. Decoding into float32 can round differently from encoding/json (#884, open).

Always pass a pointer when you marshal an ast.Node through encoding/json. Also call PretouchMany at init for large or deep types, and tune option.WithCompileMaxInlineDepth or WithCompileRecursiveDepth if JIT compilation is slow.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Pick Sonic over go-json and jsoniter on amd64 when payloads are generic (interface{}/map) or large. In the README, generic decode takes 66.8 µs vs 88.6 µs for go-json and 91.3 µs for jsoniter, and large binding decode runs at 594 vs 88 MB/s for go-json. Prefer go-json for small or medium struct-binding decode and on arm64: it matches or beats Sonic's std mode in the README (28.7 vs 32.6 µs) and in tegridy-benchie at 1-4 threads. Prefer easyjson when code generation is acceptable and you want no runtime JIT.
verified_claims_summary: The README's 13 KB, 300+ key document was benchmarked with std-equivalent options (encode: SortMapKeys|EscapeHTML|CompactMarshaler; decode: CopyString) on Go 1.17.1, darwin/amd64, Intel i9-9880H, using scripts/bench.sh with -benchtime=100000x. Sonic ran generic encode 3.3x, generic decode 1.9x and struct decode 3.4x faster than encoding/json, and parallel struct encode 2.5x. The 3.1x parallel figure uses the Fast path, which skips sorting and escaping, so it is not a like-for-like comparison. An independent 2026 run (sonic v1.15.4, i7-6820HQ, 39.9 MB SEC corpus) found about 1.8-2.0x over encoding/json.
status_note: Actively maintained by ByteDance/CloudWeGo: v1.15.4 was released 2026-09-11 and Go 1.27 support landed July 2026. The Apache-2.0 module is easy to adopt, but every new Go release needs a matching Sonic update because it depends on private runtime internals.
